params.question: A pregnant woman presents with vaginal bleeding at 10 weeks of amenorrhoea. The cervical os is closed, the uterus corresponds to dates, and no tissue has been passed. Which type of abortion does this presentation represent?

answers.text: Inevitable abortion

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: In inevitable abortion, the cervical os is open and bleeding is significant. The closed os in this patient rules out inevitable abortion.

answers.text: Threatened abortion

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. A closed cervical os, uterus matching gestational age, no tissue passage, and no signs of infection characterise threatened abortion. About half of these pregnancies continue successfully.

answers.text: Missed abortion

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: In missed abortion, the fetus has died but has not been expelled. Although the os is also closed, the uterus is typically smaller than expected for dates, and there is usually little or no active bleeding.

answers.text: Incomplete abortion

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incomplete abortion involves partial expulsion of products of conception with an open cervical os. This patient has a closed os and no tissue passage.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the four clinical anchors: os status (open or closed), uterine size relative to dates, whether tissue has passed, and whether infection is present. A closed os with bleeding but no tissue loss points to threatened abortion.
The four clinical anchors — cervical os status, uterine size, tissue passage, and infection — allow you to classify abortion type even before ultrasound is available.

interactions.label: For first-trimester incomplete abortion, which evacuation approach is now prefer

params.question: For first-trimester incomplete abortion, which evacuation approach is now preferred over sharp curettage based on randomised trial evidence and WHO guidance?

answers.text: Expectant management with serial ultrasonography

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Expectant management may be suitable for threatened or missed abortion, but incomplete abortion with retained tissue generally requires active intervention to prevent haemorrhage and infection.

answers.text: Dilatation and sharp curettage under general anaesthesia

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Sharp curettage was the traditional approach, but it carries higher risks of uterine perforation and Asherman syndrome. Current evidence and WHO guidance favour safer alternatives.

answers.text: Manual vacuum aspiration or medical management with misoprostol

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Randomised trials and WHO guidance show that manual vacuum aspiration and misoprostol are effective, safer alternatives to sharp curettage for incomplete abortion, with lower complication rates.

answers.text: Hysterotomy with direct removal of retained products

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Hysterotomy is a major abdominal procedure reserved for rare and exceptional circumstances, not a first-line approach for incomplete abortion.

overallFeedback.feedback: Current WHO guidance recommends manual vacuum aspiration or misoprostol over sharp curettage for incomplete abortion, based on randomised trial evidence showing better safety profiles.
The shift from sharp curettage to vacuum aspiration and medical management represents one of the most important evidence-based changes in early pregnancy care.

params.question: The American Society for Reproductive Medicine requires three or more consecutive pregnancy losses before 20 weeks to define recurrent pregnancy loss.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: This is false. The ASRM requires only two or more ultrasound-confirmed losses, not three. The three-consecutive-losses definition is used by the RCOG and ESHRE. ASRM lowered the threshold because even two losses cause significant emotional distress and a treatable cause can often be found.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct. The ASRM uses a lower threshold of two or more ultrasound-confirmed losses, reasoning that even two losses cause significant distress and that treatable causes can often be identified early. The three-or-more consecutive losses definition belongs to the RCOG and ESHRE.

interactions.label: Why is shoulder tip pain considered a red flag in a woman with suspected ectopic

params.question: Why is shoulder tip pain considered a red flag in a woman with suspected ectopic pregnancy?

answers.text: It indicates cervical excitation from adnexal pathology

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Cervical excitation is a separate finding elicited during bimanual pelvic examination. Shoulder tip pain has a different mechanism involving diaphragmatic irritation from haemoperitoneum.

answers.text: It signifies irritation of the diaphragm by blood collecting in the peritoneal cavity

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Blood from a ruptured ectopic pregnancy pools in the subdiaphragmatic space and irritates the phrenic nerve (C3–C5), causing referred pain at the shoulder tip. This finding suggests haemoperitoneum and potential haemodynamic compromise.

answers.text: It results from vasovagal syncope triggered by acute haemorrhage

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Vasovagal reactions cause lightheadedness, pallor, and syncope, not shoulder tip pain. Shoulder tip pain specifically indicates peritoneal irritation of the diaphragm.

answers.text: It reflects referred pain from an inflamed appendix in the right iliac fossa

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Appendicitis can cause referred pain, but in the context of amenorrhoea and a positive pregnancy test, shoulder tip pain must raise suspicion for ruptured ectopic pregnancy with haemoperitoneum, not appendicitis.

overallFeedback.feedback: In ectopic pregnancy, shoulder tip pain signals haemoperitoneum — blood collecting under the diaphragm irritates the phrenic nerve (C3–C5), producing referred pain at the shoulder tip.
Shoulder tip pain in early pregnancy is a clinical alarm — it suggests blood in the peritoneal cavity irritating the diaphragm, pointing toward a ruptured ectopic pregnancy.

interactions.label: Which combination of findings is characteristic of a complete hydatidiform mole

params.question: Which combination of findings is characteristic of a complete hydatidiform mole rather than a partial mole?

answers.text: A normal-sized uterus with mildly elevated beta-hCG

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This combination is characteristic of a partial mole, not a complete mole. Partial moles often present subtly and are frequently diagnosed only on histology after curettage.

answers.text: A uterus markedly large for dates, very high beta-hCG, and passage of grape-like vesicles

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. A complete mole causes rapid trophoblastic proliferation, producing a uterus two or more weeks ahead of expected size, markedly elevated beta-hCG, and passage of characteristic grape-like vesicles, which are pathognomonic.

answers.text: An abnormal fetus visible on ultrasound with a normal beta-hCG level

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The presence of a fetus, though abnormal, is a feature of a partial mole. A complete mole has no fetal tissue and shows very high, not normal, beta-hCG levels.

answers.text: First-trimester bleeding that resolves spontaneously without intervention

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Molar pregnancies do not resolve spontaneously. Both types require evacuation, and complete moles carry a significant risk of persistent gestational trophoblastic disease requiring follow-up.

overallFeedback.feedback: A complete mole is distinguished by a uterus markedly large for dates, very high beta-hCG, and passage of grape-like vesicles. A partial mole presents more subtly, with a normal-sized uterus and mildly raised beta-hCG.

The hallmarks of a complete mole — markedly large-for-dates uterus, very high beta-hCG, and grape-like vesicles — reflect aggressive trophoblastic proliferation and carry a higher risk of persistent disease than a partial mole.

interactions.label: Hyperemesis gravidarum is a clinical diagnosis. Which set of features constitute

params.question: Hyperemesis gravidarum is a clinical diagnosis. Which set of features constitutes the diagnostic criteria?

answers.text: Nausea starting before 6 weeks of gestation with raised serum beta-hCG levels

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Early nausea and raised beta-hCG occur in normal pregnancy as well. Hyperemesis is defined by the severity of its systemic effects, not by timing or hormone levels alone.

answers.text: Intractable vomiting, weight loss exceeding 5% of pre-pregnancy weight, and ketonuria of 2+ or more

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. These three cardinal features — vomiting unresponsive to standard anti-emetics, more than 5% weight loss, and ketonuria indicating dehydration and starvation — define hyperemesis gravidarum as a clinical diagnosis.

answers.text: Haematemesis from Mallory-Weiss tears with metabolic alkalosis

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Mallory-Weiss tears are a complication of severe, repeated retching in hyperemesis, not a defining diagnostic criterion. They may occur but are not required for diagnosis.

answers.text: A PUQE score above 13 with bilateral ovarian cysts on examination

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The PUQE score is a severity grading tool for nausea and vomiting, not part of the diagnostic definition. Bilateral theca-lutein cysts are associated with gestational trophoblastic disease, not hyperemesis specifically.

overallFeedback.feedback: Hyperemesis gravidarum is defined by three features: vomiting that does not respond to standard anti-emetics, weight loss exceeding 5% of pre-pregnancy body weight, and ketonuria (2+ or higher) indicating dehydration.

The diagnostic triad of hyperemesis gravidarum — intractable vomiting, weight loss of more than 5%, and ketonuria — separates this pathological condition from the normal nausea and vomiting of pregnancy.
